messages.subject: Summary: How can I estimate parameter for the following non-linear model?
messages.subject_clean: Summary: How can I estimate parameter for the following non-linear model?
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news subscribers

I am sorry for late reply.

Question:
How can I estimate parameter for the following non-linear model? 

y ~ b2 * b1 * exp(-b0-b1*x)/(1+exp(-b0-b1*x))^2

y : binary response variable
x : explanatory variable
b2,b1,b0 : parameters 

DON MCKENZIE's advice

Use gls() and gee() in S-PLUS.

Nick Ellis's advice

fun <- function(x,b0,b1,b2) {b2 * b1 * exp(-b0-b1*x)/(1+exp(-b0-b1*x))^2}
fit <- nls(y~fun(x,b0,b1,b2), df, start=list(b0=1,b1=1,b2=1))

There are so-called self-starting functions that estimate ther own starting
values. One is SSlogis for the logistic function. Yours is the derivative of
the logistic function. You could write your own SSderivlogis self-starting
function using SSlogis as a template.

Accordingly to Nick Ellis's advice, 
I tried to use SSlogis function as templete 
in order to apply the following model. 

y ~ w * exp((xmid - input)/scal)/(scal*(1+exp((xmid - input)/scal))^2)
y     : binary variable
input : explanatory variable
w, xmid, scal : parameters

But, I can not understand the second half of this function.
I guess it describes selfstart part.

SCDlogis <- function (input, w, xmid, scal) 
{
    .expr1 <- xmid - input
    .expr3 <- exp((.expr1/scal))
    .expr4 <- 1 + .expr3
    .expr10 <- .expr4^2
    .expr11 <- (input - xmid)/(scal)^2
    .value <- w*.expr3/(scal*(.expr4)^2)
    .actualArgs <- as.list(match.call()[c("w", "xmid", "scal")])
    if (all(unlist(lapply(.actualArgs, is.name)))) {
        .grad <- array(0, c(length(.value), 3), list(NULL, c("w", 
            "xmid", "scal")))
        .grad[, "w"] <- .expr3/(scal * (.expr4)^2)
        .grad[, "xmid"] <- w*.expr3*(1-.expr3)/(scal^2 * (.expr4)^3)
        .grad[, "scal"] <- w*.expr3/(scal*(.expr4)^2)*
        (.expr11 - 1/scal - 2*.expr3*.expr11/.expr4 )
        dimnames(.grad) <- list(NULL, .actualArgs)
        attr(.value, "gradient") <- .grad
    }
    .value
}
attr(,"initial")
function (mCall, data, LHS) 
{
    xy <- data.frame(sortedXyData(mCall[["input"]], LHS, data))
    if (nrow(xy) < 4) {
        stop("Too few distinct input values to fit a logistic")
    }
    z <- xy[["y"]]
    if (min(z) <= 0) {
        z <- z - 1.05 * min(z)
    }
    z <- z/(1.05 * max(z))
    xy[["z"]] <- log(z/(1 - z))
    aux <- coef(lm(x ~ z, xy))
    pars <- 
    as.vector(
    coef(nls(y ~ w*exp((xmid - x)/scal)/(scal*(1 + exp((xmid - x)/scal))^2), 
    data = xy, start = list(xmid = aux[1], scal = aux[2]), 
        algorithm = "plinear")))
    value <- c(pars[3], pars[1], pars[2])
    names(value) <- mCall[c("w", "xmid", "scal")]
    value
}

Many thanks.

messages.subject: "importData" from Oracle extremely slow
messages.body_plain:
I tried to use the Splus function "importData" to import data from an

Oracle database view ("my_view" contains 10 columns and 2.2 million 
rows) into an Splus data frame. It works, but it is unacceptably slow 
if the filter option is used to constrain the data!

The following example creates a data frame of 10 columns and 3200 
rows by selecting from this view. It takes 5 MINUTES to complete!

df.name <- importData(
type = "oracle",
user = "username",
password = "password",
database = "",
table = "schema_name.my_view",
server = "server_name",
filter = "column_name = 'text to search for'")

The filter option can be omitted if it is hard coded into the oracle 
view definition. Then the view itself contains only 3200 rows and it 
takes only seconds to import the data! However, this procedure is not 
at all handy because the view has to be recreated for every desired 
filter.

What is the recommended procedure for using oracle data with Splus?

Details:

- Splus Version 5.0 Release 3 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.5 : 1998, 
running on a SUN ULTRA 10

- Oracle8i Enterprise Edition Release 8.1.5 running on a SUN ULTRA 30.

Thank you for any help.
Dirk

messages.subject: Online Training...No more
messages.body_plain:
All,

It used to be that MathSoft, now Insightful, offered 2 online training
courses that were quite affordable and could be done on one's own
computer in one's own time.  They were basic courses that introduced the
user to the basics of the GUI, command line, and graphics.  I just got
word I have funding to take the courses and now have the time, but I
could not find them at the S-PLUS training site.  They have been
replaced with 2 "new" public courses.  There appears to be *nothing* new
about them except they are based on S-PLUS 6 and they cost $1700 each,
and one has to travel to a specific location to take them.  Highly
inconvenient, to say the least.  If still offered, I could have taken
both online courses for ~$400 and not spent money on travel and per
diems and not taken time off from work.

It seems that Insightful has forgotten the customer in making this
unfortunate decision.  I assume there are others, like me, who have
learned S-PLUS by the seat of our pants and would like to have some
basic training to make sure we are on the right path.  Ideally, that
training would take place upon the purchase of the software.  In
reality, however, funding for such things can be hard to come by.  I
have worked to get the funding and now that I have it, I cannot take the
courses.  Neither can my co-workers.  An affordable online course would
have allowed all of us to take the training, now none of us can.
Understanding the basics in S-PLUS is critical, and I still don't
understand any of the graphics intricacies.  I am going to take the
Statistical Modeling course offered in September since that funding has
been approved, but I just have to hope that my rudimentary education in
S-PLUS will get me through it.  It seems to me Insighful should consider
their customers needs and put these 2 basic courses back online where
most of us can have access to it.  The specialized courses, like the one
I am taking in September, can keep the same format if that's what they
want to do.

If anyone feels like me, please let your voice be heard.  Nothing will
change if none of us says anything.

Thank you for your time.

messages.subject: Re: Importing ASCII data
messages.body_plain:
This file is tricky to import with S-PLUS 2000.  It needs to be imported as
formatted ASCII (FASCII), but this requires that each line of the file have
the same number of characters.  The sample file contains lines of unequal
length (where there are missing data at the end of the line) which confuses
S-PLUS.

Modifying the file to have the same number of characters per line allows
import.data to work.  I used GNU Emacs (about 2 minutes work with the handy
tools insert-rectangle and untabify) to add a column of X's to the end of
the file, thus ensuring it had the same number of characters per line:

> import.data("firstlines", "FirstLines2.txt", FileType="FASCII",
        Format="%9s,%7f,%5f,%3s,%6f,%5f,%10f,%10f,%5f,%6f,%6f,%4f,%3*",
        ColNames=c("DAY.YMD","TIME","TIDN","SIDE","Z","DIR","SPD.MPS",
                        "PSPD.MPS","DDEV","T.C","TD.C","RH","JUNK"),
        StartRow=3)
> firstlines[1:3,]
    DAY.YMD TIME TIDN SIDE  Z DIR SPD.MPS PSPD.MPS DDEV  T.C TD.C RH
1  19991226    0    1       6  NA      NA       NA   NA 10.6   NA NA
2  19991226    0    1      12 339     2.1   6.6872   27   NA   NA NA
3  19991226    0    1      54 342     4.1   9.2592   17 10.5   NA NA

An aside -- you can also use the little-known but handy vector form of the
"sep" argument to read.table to read fixed-format files, but again the
common-line-length restriction still applies:

read.table("FirstLines2.txt",
        sep=cumsum(c(1,9,7,5,3,6,5,10,10,5,6,6,4,3)),
        
col.names=c("DAY.YMD","TIME","TIDN","SIDE","Z","DIR","SPD.MPS","PSPD.MPS",
                        "DDEV","T.C","TD.C","RH","JUNK"),
        skip=2)

Having to modify the source file is hardly satisfactory, but on the bright
side it's much easier in S-PLUS 6, where importData copes with the unequal
line lengths just fine:

> importData("FirstLines.txt", "FASCII", format =
        "%9s,%7f,%5f,%3s,%6f,%5f,%10f,%10f,%5f,%6f,%6f,%4f",
        colNames = c("DAY.YMD", "tIME", "TIDN", "SIDE", "Z", "DIR", "SPD.MPS",
                 "PSPD.MPS", "DDEV", "T.C", "TD.C",     "RH"),
         startRow = 3)
    DAY.YMD TIME TIDN SIDE   Z DIR SPD.MPS PSPD.MPS DDEV  T.C TD.C RH
1  19991226    0    1        6  NA      NA       NA   NA 10.6   NA NA
2  19991226    0    1       12 339     2.1   6.6872   27   NA   NA NA
3  19991226    0    1       54 342     4.1   9.2592   17 10.5   NA NA
4  19991226    0    3        6  NA      NA       NA   NA   NA   NA NA

So you might want to try S-PLUS 6 instead (a preview release is available on
Windows).

# David Smith

--

messages.subject: Summary of Memory Error and Solution
messages.subject_clean: Summary of Memory Error and Solution
messages.body_plain:
The original question:

I'm having some problems with S-PLUS suddenly closing itself, or often
giving me the message:

The instruction at "0x5f841793" referenced memory at "0x00000036."  The
memory could not be "read."  Click OK to terminate the program.

The codes, which I assume to be memory addresses, are always the same.
The problem used to be (apparently) random, but now I can generate it
every time
with a particular plotting function that overlays an image on a map.
The function works fine in one project with one set of map limits, but
same code with different xlim and ylim on the map and moved to a
different project will generate the error every time.

S-PLUS ver 4.5 release 2, Windows 2000 Professional, 128 megs ram.

--------------------

Suggestions, results of trying them, and great thanks to everyone who
responded:

1.  It's a known Windows 2000 bug.  Upgrade to service pack 2.

  This was the first thing I tried, but it did not fix the problem.

2.  Not enough RAM.  

  I tripled the RAM in my machine today. It's too early to say what
effect that will have on the problem.  I suspect it will help.

3.  Upgrade to a newer version of S-PLUS.  

  This I may do in the near future.  I'm nervous about doing it
immediately because I'm terribly busy right now and my experience is
that in the past S-PLUS has not been entirely backwards compatible.  I
just don't have time to bother with re-coding functions that currently
function as expected!

4.  And the SOLUTION is... (Special thanks to Madeline Bauer)

Too much of your data are outside the xlim and ylim limits.  This, for
some odd reason, causes S-PLUS to eat memory.

  This was exactly the problem.  I just made my map boundaries slightly
larger so that fewer of my grid cells were ouside the map boundaries and
I'm now happily plotting away again.

Thanks! KG

--------------------------------------------------------
Kristi Gebhart, Research Physical Scientist
National Park Service, Air Resources Division
CIRA, Colorado State University
gebhart at cira.colostate.edu

messages.subject_clean: Compiling Splus contributed code for SGI with gcc
messages.body_plain:
A while ago our SGI Irix system (Irix 6.5 IP28; Splus 5.1)
was upgraded, so we no longer have access to the SGI compilers. Trying
to compile with gcc for dynamic loading in Splus with dyn.load.shared
(or even static loading) gives the error 

        'can't mix -o32 and -n32 abi'

To get this far I had to change the flags used by Splus COMPILE. Splus
is compiled with the -o32 abi, while gcc currently supports only the
newer -n32 abi. Is there a workaround?  Is this issue
likely to be resolved in the near future in future versions of Splus? Or
gcc?

Thanks,
Rod Ball

messages.body_plain:
A new version of the MASS libraries, 6.2pl007, is now available from the
master site

http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3

and shortly from the mirrors.

The reason for the announcement is that this is definitely the last ever
update for S-PLUS 3.3, 4.0 and 4.5 for Windows (we have now deleted our
last copies), and probably the last update for S3-based systems (3.x for
Unix, 2000 on Windows).

It is also the version intended to be shipped with S-PLUS 6.0 for Windows,
and a pre-compiled version that runs under the release candidates is
available at

http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/S+6/

The only non-bug-fix change recently is extra code for handling trend
surfaces contributed by Riger Bivand.

V&R4 is due in mid 2002, and will be for S-PLUS 6.0 or later (and not
earlier).

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was wondering whether anyone is able to help me. I
am trying to fit a theoretical variogram model, by
nonlinear least squares, to my data using the code in
"S+SPATIAL STATS" by Kaluzny, Vega, Cardosa and
Shelly.

My code is as follows (following page 96):

spher.fun <-
function(gamma,distance,range,sill,nugget)
gamma - spher.vgram(distance,
+ range=range,sill=sill,nugget=nugget)
MAP.nl1 <- nls( ~ spher.fun
+ (gamma,distance,range,sill,nugget),
+ data=Cape,start=list(range=0.6,sill=1000,nugget=20))
coef(MAP.nl1)

And it gives me the following error:
Error in nls( ~ spher.fun(gamma, distance, range,..:
Object "distance" not found

I have also tried the next function, in the book:
spher.wfun <- function(gammma,
+ distance,np,range,sill,nugget)
{
gammahat <- spher.vgram
+(distance,range=range,sill=sill,nugget=nugget)
sqrt(np)*(gamma/gammahat-1)
}
MAP.nl2 <- nls( ~ spher.wfun(gamma,
+ distance,np,range,sill,nugget),
+ data=Cape,start=list(range=0.6,
+ sill=1000,nugget=20))
coef(MAP.nl2)

Which also gives me the same error.

Any help or suggestions would be appreciated. Also if
anyone knows of any packages that will do cokriging,
and specifically any libraries that have been written
for R or Splus that will perform cokriging.

messages.subject: Re: Online Training...No more
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 2 Jul 2001, Winifred Lambert wrote:

> All,
> 
> It used to be that MathSoft, now Insightful, offered 2 online training
> courses that were quite affordable and could be done on one's own
> computer in one's own time.  They were basic courses that introduced the
> user to the basics of the GUI, command line, and graphics.  I just got
> word I have funding to take the courses and now have the time, but I
> could not find them at the S-PLUS training site.  

I expect basic economics is the reason that they are not offered any more.  
I used to work for MathSoft/Insightful and was one of the authors of the
web based courses (though I am no longer officially associated with
Insightful, so cannot speak for them).  When we first created the courses
we had great hopes that they would help people like you, unfortunately
they did not do as well as we had initially hoped and there was some worry
that the money coming in from them would not cover the cost of hosting
them (at the time we used third party software with an anual licence fee
to deal with granting access only to paying customers, navigating through
the course, etc.).  The fact that they are no longe available indicates
that they probably did not make the money to cover the yearly fee.

If you know for certain that there is a market for them now, let
Insightful know and maybe they will offer them again.  Another
possibility, if there are several people at your company interested in
taking the course Insightful may be willing to sell you a copy of the
original html files for internal use.

--

messages.subject: Trellis question
messages.body_plain:
I have 18 sheep and for each I have two physiological measures of the
heart (Ved and logPed) which I'd like to plot against one another in the
scenarios of NSR and AFIB.

Using the superimpose trellis function, I can make this happen:

xyplot(logPed~Ved|factor(Animal),data=all,aspect=1,
groups=group,pch=c(1,2),panel=panel.superpose,strip=remove.shading.fun(),as.table=T)

Here, of course, logPed is on the y-axis, Ved is on the x-axis, I see one
plot for each of the 18 sheep, and point type differs between NSR and
AFIB.  Perfect.

Now, however, I'd like to add the best fit line for each scenario.

I know how to do this with just one group:

xyplot(logPed~Ved|factor(Animal),data=all,aspect=1,strip=remove.shading.fun(),as.table=T,panel=function(x,y,
...)  {panel.xyplot(x,y,...,col=1)
panel.abline(lm(y~x, na.action=na.omit),lty=2)})

But I can't figure out how to make the first plot with two best-fit lines,
one for each group.

Can someone please advise me how to add two ablines, one for each group,
on the plot where I've used panel.superpose?

Thank you very much.

        Jason

messages.subject: Re: Clustering with Mahanalobis distance
messages.body_plain:
>  -----Original Message-----
> From:         Lidia Rejto [mailto:rejto at renyi.hu] 
> Sent: Friday, 6 July 2001 1:29 PM
> To:   s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> Subject:      [S] Clustering with Mahanalobis distance
> 
> 
> Hello:
> 
> Is anybody used  Splus clustering with Mahanalobis distance?
> What should I do to use k-means with Mahanalobis distance?

Suppose you have your observations as the rows of the matrix X and V is the
variance matrix relative to which you wish to calculate Mahalanobis
distances.  Then putting

        Z = X V^{-1/2}

(where V^{-1/2} is any matrix square root) and doing k-means on Z is
equivalent to doing k-means on X with distances between rows defined by the
Mahalanobis metric.

If V is in fact the variance matrix defined by X (after subtracting the
mean, say) then you can choose Z as svd(scale(X, scale=F))$u and use k-means
with that.  If your mean structure is a little more complicated, just use a
projection onto the residual space, of course.

(Warning: do a little matrix algebra on it first just to check.  It's good
for you!)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: Clustering with Mahanalobis distance
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 6 Jul 2001, Lidia Rejto wrote:

>    Is anybody used  Splus clustering with Mahanalobis distance?
> What should I do to use k-means with Mahanalobis distance?

There has been an example of that in V&R in the past, I believe.  You need
to transform the space so that the Euclidean distance is the Mahanalobis
distance, by the inverse of a square root of the matrix.

That's assuming you know the matrix in advance: it should be something
similar to the within-cluster covariance matrix.  For the
covariance matrix of the whole population, the procedure is equivalent to
transforming to principal components and re-scaling each to unit variance.

Dear S-group;

I am trying to compare several commercial and shareware clustering programs 
(k-means, SOM, HMM) to the built-in S+ clustering algorithms using a standard 
normalized symmetrical similarity matrix that I created from a BLAST algorithm. 
 Question: has anyone written code to output a simple list of cluster ownership 
and row name?  All the S+ clustering algorithms give me a different type of 
output for group membership.  Also, has anyone out there written an HMM in S

messages.subject: Re: Robust linear model with t distribution
messages.subject_clean: Robust linear model with t distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

perhaps the following article may be interesting:

\item[] {\rm Lange, K.L., Little, R.J.A. and Taylor, J.M.G.} (1989).
  Robust statistical modelling using the t distribution.
  {\em J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.}, {\bf 84}, 881-886.

It is mainly concentrated on the maximum likelihood approach.
The authors  show that it can be very difficult (if the data set is
not huge) to estimate the degrees of freedom parameter
from the t-distribution with reasonable precision.
Often it seems to be better to define this
parameter to a small fixed constant , say 3 or 4, at least from
a robustness point of view.

Andreas Christmann

Andreas Christmann wrote:

<snip> 

> \item[] {\rm Lange, K.L., Little, R.J.A. and Taylor, J.M.G.} (1989).
>   Robust statistical modelling using the t distribution.
>   {\em J. Amer. Statist. Assoc.}, {\bf 84}, 881-886.

> The authors  show that it can be very difficult (if the data set is
> not huge) to estimate the degrees of freedom parameter
> from the t-distribution with reasonable precision.

This point, in particular, is noted in

(1999) Fernandez, C and Steel, M. F. J
Multivariate Student t-regression models: Pitfalls and inference
Biometrika, 86. pp 153-167

In this paper it states that the estimates for the degrees of freedom
found in Lange et al (1989) correspond to local rather than global
maxima and that it is not clear how to optimise such a parameter. As 
Andreas said....

> "Often it seems to be better to define this
> parameter to a small fixed constant , say 3 or 4, at least from
> a robustness point of view."

Ken Kelley <KKelley at ND.Edu> wrote:

> Hello everyone,
> 
> I have  been becoming  interested in noncentral  distributions, namely
> those of the t, F, and chi sq distributions.  I would guess that there
> is a way  in S-Plus to derive the quantiles  of these distributions if
> one knows  the degrees of  freedom and noncentrality  parameter value.
> However, I have been unable to  locate information on how one would go
> about finding  these quantiles.  Is there even  a way to do  this in S
> Plus?  If not what would other options be to obtaining these values?
> 
> I'm using  S-Plus 2000 Professional  on Windows 98SE.  Thanks  for any
> help and have a nice day, Ken
> 

The calculations  are not totally trivial  and, as far as  I know, are
not built  in to Splus.  We  have Fortran 77 and  C code (mechanically
translated  from F77) for  these computations.   We have  not packaged
this code for  S, but it should not be too  difficult.  If anyone does
this, please post the results to Statlib or me.

Brian Ripley has packaged the noncentral t -- see
             www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/S/noncent.sh.gz

We are  working on an improved  F95 packaging of the  routines for the
cdfs, inverses, and more of common stat routines.  At the moment, it's
a work  in progress and I  am not sure how  F95 connects with  S if at
all.

Announcing a new course:

########
This two-day course gives a detailed overview of statistical
models for data mining, inference and prediction.
With the rapid developments in internet technology, genomics and
other high tech industries, we rely increasingly more on  data analysis
and statistical models to exploit the vast amounts of data
at our fingertips. 

This sequel to our popular Modern Regression and Classification course
covers many new areas of unsupervised learning and data mining,
and  gives an in-depth treatment of some of the hottest tools
in supervised learning.

The first course is not a pre-requisite for this new course.

Day one focusses on state-of-art  methods for supervised
learning including PRIM, boosting and support vector machines.
Day  two covers unsupervised learning including clustering,
principal components, principal curves and  self-organizing maps.
Many applications will be discussed, including DNA expression arrays.
These are one of the hottest new areas in biology!

  Elements of Statistical Learning: data mining, inference and prediction 

(with J. Friedman, Springer -Verlag, 2001).

messages.subject: substring with different formats
messages.body_plain:
I posted a question regarding extending the function substring.   
I will repeat my question

and put the only response that I received.

 

Q:

I was wondering if anyone had extended the * substring * command to 
allow for something

like this:

 

x <- c("Alabama, Northern", "Alaska", "Georgia, Southern")

unpaste( x, ",")

 

[[1]] "Alabama"  "Alaska"  "Georgia"

[[2]] "Northern" "NA"  "Southern"

 

In other words, extending unpaste to the case in which the separtor does 
not exist for all

observations.

 

A: (S.D. Byers)

In perl there is a function called qw. It does exactly that. I 
wrote an
Splus equivalent some time ago:

qw <- function(x) { 
unlist(string.break.line(translate(x, " ", "\n"))) }

This mandates 
you  have the translate function but  you could probably
rewrite 
to  get around that.  Or just use the  string.break.line 
thing
more directly.

Example:

S+> qw("Monday Tuesday 
Wednesday Thursday Friday Sauturday 
Sunday")
        
1         
2           
3          
4        
5           
6        7
 "Monday" "Tuesday" 
"Wednesday" "Thursday" "Friday" "Sauturday" "Sunday"

messages.subject: new solution to problem with unpaste
messages.subject_clean: new solution to problem with unpaste
messages.body_plain:
Here is a self contained function that extends the 
function * unpaste *

which was written by Samuel Buttrey.

 

This works on your example but won't work 
for the more general case where the separator might appear more than once in a 
string. That I leave to you.
 

Start 
by defining the function any.sep(), which determines which strings contain the 
separator. By the way, this is best viewed in a fixed-width font like 
Courier.

 

> any.sep
function(strs, sep = 
",")
{
 result <- rep(F, length(strs))    # 
set up logical vector as result
 for(i in 1:length(strs)) 
{        # go through 
strings
  this.str <- 
strs[i]                # 
break each into individual characters
  chars <- 
substring(this.str, 1:nchar(this.str), 
1:nchar(this.str))
  result[i] <- any(chars == 
sep)    # return T if sep appears 

 }
 result
}

 

Now instead of unpaste(), use 
newunpaste().

> newunpaste
function(strs, sep = ",")
{
 out <- 
unpaste(strs, sep)        # do regular 
unpaste
 nosep <- !any.sep(strs, sep)    # 
identify strings without sep...
 out[[1]][nosep] <- 
strs[nosep]    # ...and put those values into 
"out"
 out
}

 

Example, using your "x":
> newunpaste 
(x)
[[1]]:
[1] "Alabama" "Alaska"  "Georgia"

 

[[2]]:
[1] " Northern" 
"NA"        " Southern"

 

Warning messages:
  wrong number of fields in 
entry(ies) 2 in: unpaste(strs, sep)
> 

Note the warning, which comes from unpaste(); you might 
or might not want to suppress that. Note also the spaces at the front of 
"Northern" and "Southern"; that's a consequence of how unpaste() 
works.

messages.subject: Summary Re: !is.na and "Badly placed ()'s"
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to the 20+ people who've responded with
similar solutions:

The character "!" at the Splus prompt is interpretted
as an escape to the shell, and it is the shell which returned 
the error message.
Enclosing the command in parentheses or brackets

messages.subject_clean: Summary: combine duplicated rows in a big data set
messages.body_plain:
s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu 
         
Dear Splus users,

I want to thank Peter Geddes, Patrick Connolly, Nick
Ellis for their responses. I end up using 
Dunlap's "agg.sum" function.It works great for big
data sets. Below are their answers:

1.Peter showed me his codes, but written in Euphoria.
So I will omit them here. 

2. Patrick: I think tapply with an index made by
pasting values from V1 and V2 and
sum as your function being applied will do the trick.

tapply(M1$V3,paste(M1$V1,M1$2),sum

3. Nick forwarded an old email in this archive to me.
It has the agg.sum function. 

"unname" <- function(x)
{
# Author : Bill Dunlap, from MathSoft.
# Date   : ???
# Purpose: will remove the name from it's argument
"x".

 names(x)<-NULL
 x
}

"agg.sum"<-
function(x, by, sort.it = T)
{
     if(!is.data.frame(by))
          by <- data.frame(by)
     if(sort.it) {
          ord <- do.call("order", unname(by))
          x <- x[ord]
          by <- by[ord,  ]
     }
     logical.diff <- function(group)
     group[-1] != group[ - length(group)]
     change <- logical.diff(by[[1]])
     for(i in seq(along = by)[-1])
          change <- change | logical.diff(by[[i]])
     by <- by[c(T, change),  , drop = F]
     by$x <- diff(c(0, cumsum(x)[c(change, T)]))
     by
}

for the details, you can find a post titled "[S]
Re:Summary: Alternatives to aggregate "  in the "Dec
1999" folder.

Below is my original question:

Dear Splus Users,

When handling a big data set ( 200K * 26 ), I come
across this problem. The data set ( M1 )looks like
this:

4  B  Z  6

that is, I need to add up the V3's for rows with the

in M1. 

Could anyone tell me how to do it efficiently?

Thank you.

Haibo

messages.subject: conf intervals for logistic regr predictions
messages.subject_clean: conf intervals for logistic regr predictions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus
(working with Splus2000 and Win98)
I'm trying to compute predictions and 95%ci's from logistic regression
models. The models may have factors as independent variables and may
contain polynomials. My aim is to be able to do the predictions etc in
ArcInfo (GIS software) because I'm predicting to large data sets. I realise
I can't simply use the Splus coefficients outside of splus. My strategy is
to build a data frame for prediction that is representative of the range of
each variable, and predict to that inside Splus, then use it as a look-up
table in ArcInfo. I think I've managed ok for the predictions but am stuck
with the standard errors. I'd appreciate any comments on this.

This is what seems to work for predictions:
newdat is a dataframe that has 100 rows dedicated to the ranges of each
variable across the whole region for prediction, and 2 extra rows that act
as a test - they each have a new combination of values for the variables
that is not represented in that combination elsewhere in the data frame. 

test6<-predict.gam(mymodel,newdat,type="response")
test6[102]
         102 
0.0007164527  ...........ie this is an example of one of my checkpoints

test5<-predict.gam(mymodel,newdat,type="terms")

test7.102<-attributes(test5)$constant+ sum(test5[102,])
exp(test7.102)/(1 + exp(test7.102))
[1] 0.0007164527             ...........ie the method works within the new
rows

test8.102<-attributes(test5)$constant + test5[,1][newdat[,1]==100][1] +
test5[,2][newdat[,2]==11.1][1] + test5[,3][newdat[,3]==103][1] +
test5[,4][newdat[,4]==5.1][1] + test5[,5][newdat[,5]==4][1] +
test5[,6][newdat[,6]==3200][1] + test5[,7][newdat[,7]==1820][1] +
test5[,8][newdat[,8]==1][1] + test5[,9][newdat[,9]==22.5][1]
> exp(test8.102)/(1 + exp(test8.102))
          102 
 0.0007164527 ..........ie the method works for combinations of data picked
throughout the dataframe, and this simulates what will be done in ArcInfo

My question is whether the above is a correct interpretation of how the
"terms" matrix can be used, but more importantly what I can do about
standard errors. I'm not sure what the standard errors of the terms
represent. If I try to treat them in the same way as I've treated the
predictions I don't get results I'd expect:

#firstly this is how I would normally compute an upper 95% ci inside splus:
test10<-predict.gam(mymodel,newdat,type="link",se.fit=T)
temp102<-test10$fit[102] + 1.96*test10$se.fit[102]
exp(temp102)/(1 + exp(temp102))
 0.9003377   .............ie this is the "reference" result

#this attempts a (too simple?) interpretation of the terms' se's:
test9<-predict.gam(mymodel,newdat,type="terms",se.fit=T)
test11.102<-attributes(test9$fit)$constant + sum(test9$fit[102,]) +
sum(1.96*test9$se.fit[102,])
exp(test11.102)/(1 + exp(test11.102))
[1] 0.9964148 ..........ie a different result!

..and I get this same answer (0.996..) if I pick the data from all over the
data frame of the terms matrix, as I did for the predictions in the first
section. 

My suspicion is that these standard errors can't be interpreted in this
way. I would like to understand them and to be shown an alternative
approach as a solution for creating confidence intervals on predictions
outside splus. Thanks very much in advance for any comments

sincerely
Jane Elith

j.elith at botany.unimelb.edu.au

messages.subject: Summary: Importing ASCII data
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the late summary.

I had a problem importing an ASCII file that was formatted in columns,
but the data did not import into the correct columns in S-PLUS if there
were missing data in columns at the end of a record.

I got responses from Shawn Boles, Bert Gunter, Don McKenzie, David
Smith, and James Holtman.  The problem was that each line of the file
did not have the same number of characters.  In the rows that had
missing data in the columns at the end of the line, the trailing blanks
were stripped.  According to David Smith, this confused S-PLUS.  If I
wanted the data to be in the correct columns in S-PLUS, I had to pad
each of the lines data with blanks at the end so that every line had the
same number of characters.

Suggestions were to use read.table(), scan(), make.fields(), and
import.data(), but they required lines of the same length.  David
suggesting using a GNU Emacs script to do this before importing the
data, but I wanted to do it all in S-PLUS.

I appreciate everyone's suggestions, but James Holtman gets the gold
star for providing the exact sequence of function calls that I need.
They will fit nicely into a script file that I can run automatically to
read in all my files.  Here is what he sent:

# THESE VALUES WILL BE USED LATER IN SCAN()
# x.what IS THE LIST OF VECTOR NAMES
# x.width IS THE CHARACTER WIDTH OF EACH OF THE COLUMNS
> x.what <- list(date=0, time=0, tidh=0, side='', z=0, dir=0, spd=0,
pspd=0, ddev=0, tc=0, tdc=0, rh=0)
> x.width <- c(9,7,5,5,4,5,10,10,5,6,6,4)

# READ IN THE FILE
> x.1 <- scan('firstline.txt',what='',sep='\n')

# DETERMINE THE NUMBER OF CHARACTERS PER LINE
> nchar(x.1)
 [1] 76 76 66 60 66 30 30 30 30 30 76 60 76 60 60 66 76 60 76 60 60 76
30 30 60 30 30 76 60 76 60 76 76 60 76 60 76

# MAX NUMBER OF CHARACTERS IS 76 FOR LINES WITH NO MISSING DATA
# PAD LINES WITH LESS THAN 76 CHARACTERS WITH TRAILING BLANKS
> x.2 <- substring(paste(x.1,'
'),1,76)

# NOW CHECK TO MAKE SURE ALL THE LINES HAVE 76 CHARACTERS
> nchar(x.2)
 [1] 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76
76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76 76

# WRITE() THE FILE AND SCAN() IT INTO A NEW OBJECT WITH THE COLUMN
WIDTHS AND THE VECTOR NAMES
> write(x.2)
> x.1 <- scan('data',what=x.what,width=x.width,skip=2)

messages.subject: Re: partial autocorrelation within groups
messages.body_plain:
I received one reply to my query (at the bottom of this message) about
computing partial autocorrelations for models fitted by lme and gls.  The
following function, submitted by Rolf Turner, allows one to compute the
empirical partial autocorrelation function of within-groups residuals from
the autocorrelations.  I have added PACF, PACF.lme, PACF.gls, and plot.PACF
to facilitate plotting.  (These are completely analogous to the functions
ACF, ACF.lme, ACF.gls, and plot.ACF).  These functions work in SPlus 5.1
with nlme package version 3.3.

durb.lev <- function(rho,k=NULL) {
#
# Function durb.lev to apply the Durbin-Levinson algorithm
# to calculate the ***partial*** autocorrelations from the
# autocorrelations.
#
if(any(abs(rho) > 1)) stop("rho is not an autocorrelation vector")
if(is.null(k)) k <- length(rho)
phi <- matrix(0,k,k)
phi[1,1] <- rho[1]
for(i in 2:k) {
        i1 <- i-1
        ind <- 1:i1
        tb <- rho[i] - sum(phi[i1,ind]*rho[rev(ind)])
        bb <- 1 - sum(phi[i1,ind]*rho[ind])
        phi[i,i] <- tb/bb
        if(i<k) for(j in ind) phi[i,j] <- phi[i1,j] - phi[i,i]*phi[i1,i-j]
}
diag(phi)
}

PACF <-
## partial autocorrelation function
function(object, maxLag, ...)
UseMethod("PACF")

PACF.lme <-
function(object, maxLag, resType = c("pearson", "response", "normalized"),
 ...)
{
 resType <- match.arg(resType)
 res <- resid(object, type = resType, asList = TRUE)
 if(missing(maxLag)) {
  maxLag <- min(c(maxL <- max(sapply(res, length)) - 1,
   as.integer(10 * log10(maxL + 1))))
 }
 val <- lapply(res, function(el, maxLag)
 {
  N <- maxLag + 1
  tt <- double(N)
  nn <- integer(N)
  N <- min(c(N, n <- length(el)))
  nn[1:N] <- n + 1 - 1:N
  ## el <- el - mean(el)
  for(i in 1:N) {
   tt[i] <- sum(el[1:(n - i + 1)] * el[i:n])
  }
  array(c(tt, nn), c(length(tt), 2))
 }
 , maxLag = maxLag)
 val0 <- apply(sapply(val, function(x)
 x[, 2]), 1, sum)
 val1 <- apply(sapply(val, function(x)
 x[, 1]), 1, sum)/val0
 val2 <- val1/val1[1]
 z <- data.frame(lag = 0:maxLag, ACF = val2)
 attr(z, "n.used") <- val0
 z$PACF <- c(1, durb.lev(z$ACF[-1]))
 oldClass(z) <- "PACF"
 z
}

PACF.gls <-
function(object, maxLag, resType = c("pearson", "response", "normalized"),
 form =  ~ 1, na.action = na.fail, ...)
{
 resType <- match.arg(resType)
 res <- resid(object, type = resType)
 wchRows <- NULL
 if(is.null(grps <- getGroups(object))) {
  ## check if formula defines groups
  if(!is.null(grpsF <- getGroupsFormula(form))) {
   if(is.null(data <- getData(object))) {
    ## will try to construct
    allV <- all.vars(grpsF)
    if(length(allV) > 0) {
     alist <- lapply(as.list(allV), as.name)
     names(alist) <- allV
     alist <- c(as.list(as.name("data.frame"
      )), alist)
     mode(alist) <- "call"
     data <- eval(alist, sys.parent(1))
    }
   }
   grps <- model.frame(grpsF, data, na.action = na.action)
   wchRows <- !is.na(match(row.names(data), row.names(
    grps)))
   grps <- getGroups(grps, grpsF)
  }
 }
 if(!is.null(grps)) {
  if(!is.null(wchRows)) {
   res <- res[wchRows]
  }
  res <- split(res, grps)
 }
 else {
  res <- list(res)
 }
 if(missing(maxLag)) {
  maxLag <- min(c(maxL <- max(sapply(res, length)) - 1,
   as.integer(10 * log10(maxL + 1))))
 }
 val <- lapply(res, function(el, maxLag)
 {
  N <- maxLag + 1
  tt <- double(N)
  nn <- integer(N)
  N <- min(c(N, n <- length(el)))
  nn[1:N] <- n + 1 - 1:N
  ## el <- el - mean(el)
  for(i in 1:N) {
   el1 <- el[1:(n - i + 1)]
   el2 <- el[i:n]
   tt[i] <- sum(el1 * el2)
  }
  array(c(tt, nn), c(length(tt), 2))
 }
 , maxLag = maxLag)
 val0 <- apply(sapply(val, function(x)
 x[, 2]), 1, sum)
 val1 <- apply(sapply(val, function(x)
 x[, 1]), 1, sum)/val0
 val2 <- val1/val1[1]
 z <- data.frame(lag = 0:maxLag, ACF = val2)
 attr(z, "n.used") <- val0
 z$PACF <- c(1, durb.lev(z$ACF[-1]))
 oldClass(z) <- "PACF"
 z
}

plot.PACF <-
function(object, alpha = 0, xlab = "Lag", ylab = "Partial autocorrelation",
 grid = FALSE, ...)
{
 ylim <- range(object$PACF)
 if(alpha) {
  assign("stdv", qnorm(1 - alpha/2)/sqrt(attr(object, "n.used")),
   frame = 1)
  stMax <- max(stdv)
  ylim <- c(min(c( - stMax, ylim[1])), max(c(ylim[2], stMax)))
 }
 assign("alpha", as.logical(alpha), frame = 1)
 assign("grid", grid, frame = 1)
 xyplot(PACF ~ lag, object, ylim = ylim, panel = function(x, y)
 {
  if(grid)
   panel.grid()
  panel.xyplot(x, y, type = "h")
  panel.abline(0, 0)
  if(alpha) {
   lines(x, stdv, lty = 2)
   lines(x,  - stdv, lty = 2)
  }
 }
 , xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, ...)
}
>

Jack Lewis wrote:

> With models fitted by lme and gls, ACF.lme() and ACF.gls() give the
> empirical autocorrelation function of within-groups residuals [nlme
> package version 3.3], but not the partial autocorrelations.  Yet both
> are needed for ARMA model identification.  Has anyone written a function
> to calculate the partial autocorrelations?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Jack Lewis
>

> unsubscribe send e-mail to s-news-request at lists.biostat.wustl.edu with
> the BODY of the message:  unsubscribe s-news

messages.subject: Re: Calling lme (How DOES S-Plus work anyway)
messages.subject_clean: Calling lme (How DOES S-Plus work anyway)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

I'm not sure why you are getting this error. 

The following methods for substituting in a fixedpart work for me [Splus
6.0 on SunOS 5.6, NLME version 3.3]: 

Method 1:
fixedpart<-formula(y~x-1)
lme1<-lme(fixedpart,random=~1|group,data=Data,na.action=na.omit)

Method 2:
fixedpart<-"y~x-1"
lme2<-lme(eval(parse(text=fixedpart)),random=~1|group,data=Data,na.action=na.omit)

I think Method 2 is a bit more flexible.  When I've automagically
generated formulae for models, I've used paste() and
eval(parse(text="formula")) to feed the formulae to the relevant function.
For example, if I wanted to run 3 models (say, y~x1,y~x2,y~x3), I could
do: 

fixedparts<-paste("y~x",1:3,sep="")
models<-paste("lme",1:3,sep="")

for(i in 1:3){
assign(models[i],lme(eval(parse(text=fixedparts[i])),data=Data,random=~1|group),where=1,immediate=T)
}

Using assign(,where=1,immediate=T) makes sure that the objects
lme1,lme2, and lme3 get written into the working .Data directory.

Anyway, I hope this helps.

Best,

Jake
------------
Jake Bowers
Dept of Political Science
UC-Berkeley

Dear S+ Users,

I want to thank Peter Ellis and Andy Liaw for their
quick responses.
In the end, I used Andy's way, which gave more
control.

Andy : When a sequence of plots are generated
"on-the-fly", each new plot will
overwrite the previous one.  There's no easy way to
get around this 
(that I
know of anyway) other than setting par(ask=T) before
plotting.  This 
way,
you will be prompted to press [enter] before the next
plot is drawn.

On Windows, the "graphsheet" device can have "tabbed"
pages, so 
different
plots will show up on a different tab sheet.  I think
in the new Splus 
6 for
Unix, the java.graph() device also has tabbed sheets. 
(If you run 
Splus in
a terminal, you will need the -j option to get the
Java device.  The 
Java
device is the default device if you use the Java GUI
(-g option), I 
think.)

Haibo

messages.body_plain:
Dear All

Which is better, R and S? Since a researcher suggests me that it may be an
embarrassing question, I would like to comment why I am interested in the
question. Some of readers in this mailing list may know that I currently
struggled to do a double integration with S-plus. My case is not simple
double integration because the function and integration range is nested and
a trouble of scooping variables occurred. For this problem, a researcher
kindly points out;

"I had similar problem before. What I was feeling is that the modification
of the single integrate function for calculating double integration is not
very reliable. This is due to the scope method used in Splus. If you use R,
you can easily modify a single integration function to calculate a double
integration. Also, there is a package called 'Swin' at the s dos/windows
collection in statlib, which contained a double integrate function. It works
very well."

By this response, I am truly interested in the difference of R and S.
Therefore, I asked the same question to a student in my room. He replied
that R runs faster a litter bit than S. Is it really true?  I just want to
know the general impression about the difference of R and S from the users,
and don't intend to criticize neither of software.

Best wishes,
Takashi Kikuchi

On Fri, 13 Jul 2001, Dr. Takashi Kikuchi wrote:

> R is almost same as S languag but what is the difference actually between
> two when we make a programming? I want to read a book or reference

Could you try asking your colleagues first?  (Many of your fellow students
use both, including the one sitting to your left.)

Venables & Ripley (2000) `S Programming'

is probably what you are looking for.  See also the R FAQ (which ships with
R).

One stance is that S version 3 (as in S-PLUS 2000, 4.x, 3.x), S version 4
(as in S-PLUS 5.x and 6.x) and R are all dialects of the S language.  There
are major differences between the Sv3 and Sv4, so the `S language' is
not really at all well defined.

messages.subject: Re: synchronizing batch processes
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 16 Jul 2001, Carlisle Thacker wrote:

> I have too many data to fit into memory, so I have to treat them in
> groups.  I have built a unix script that loops over the groups,
> accessing the appropriate data from the database and then running
> Splus in batch mode.  It seems that the Splus process is running in
> the background and that control is returned to the unix script,
> causing the data access to be out of sync with the processing.
>
> Any hints on how I can control the timing?  Where should I read?

Just make your own script.  BATCH is

gannet% cat BATCH
case $#
in
2)      BATCH=yes; export BATCH
        S_BATCH_INPUT=$1; S_BATCH_OUTPUT=$2; export S_BATCH_INPUT S_BATCH_OUTPUT
        (echo "invisible(options(echo=TRUE))"; cat $1)| nohup Splus >$2
2>&1 &
        ;;
*)      echo "Usage:
Splus BATCH inputfile outputfile"
        ;;
esac

and I used (for S+3.4)

#!/bin/sh
OUT=${2-s3/$1.out}
BATCH=yes; export BATCH
S_BATCH_INPUT=$1; S_BATCH_OUTPUT=$2; export S_BATCH_INPUT S_BATCH_OUTPUT
rm -rf .Data
mkdir .Data
(echo "invisible(options(echo=T,width=65,digits=5)); assign('lib.loc',
'../../soft', w=0)"; \
    cat $1; echo "memory.size(max=T);proc.time();date()") \
    | Splus >${OUT} 2>&1

when running the VR scripts.  Note the crucial missing final `&'.

I have no idea if

BATCH=yes; export BATCH
S_BATCH_INPUT=$1; S_BATCH_OUTPUT=$2; export S_BATCH_INPUT S_BATCH_OUTPUT

is actually needed: some experiments suggested not.

messages.subject_clean: Reading certain part of text file
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 16 Jul 2001, Ahmet Turhan wrote:

> Dear Friends,
>
> Is there any way to read just certain part of data? Like between line 5 to
> line10. read.table skips certain number of line but continues until last
> line. Any help appreciated.

1) Use scan() and set nmax or nlines (depending on what you want done with
blank lines).

2) Make a temporary copy of those lines and use read.table.  For example
using R 1.3.0

inp <- file("myfile.dat", "r")
out <- file(, "rw")
junk <- readLines(inp, 4)
writeLines(readLines(inp, 6), out)
ans <- read.table(out)
close(inp); close(out)

There are slicker ways using pushbacks on connections, but those are
much harder to explain.  This one is subtle enough (it uses an anonymous
file opened for both reading and writing).

--

messages.subject: Summary:Matlab > Splus?
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

I would like to thank Andy Liaw, Matt Kurbat, Randy
Norsworthy,Claudio Verzilli and Andrew Sinclair for
their responses to my question about Matlab and Splus.
(by the way,I joined this news group about one week
ago, and I love it. The responses are fast and
right-to-the-point.)  Here are parts of their
comments:

1. Andy Liaw:

I believe in general looping in Matlab is more
efficient (both in time and memory) than in Splus. 
There are, however, many other important differences. 
The statistics functionality in Matlab is
embarrassingly primitive, but its signal and image
processing capabilities run rings around Splus.  There
are no such a thing as data frame, which makes 
even simple analysis of mixed-type data sets a bit
challenging.

2. Matt Kurbat: 

Here's an analogy: 

Matlab:math:: splus: statistics

of course, math and statistics have overlap, so splus
and matlab do too.but splus is stronger than matlab on
statistics, whereas matlab is stronger on areas of
math other than statistics (e.g., numerical linear
algebra).

3.Randy Norsworthy:

It depends on what you want to do. Both packages have
wavelets capability,which we use here, as well as lots
of other capacity. The interchange among users it
better supported in S-Plus. There are probably more 
non-statistical applications available for Matlab. In
any case, the time cost of programming a serious
application from scratch in either package is
prohibitive,compared to the efficiency of either in
executing existing code. Forget "faster." The
important issues, as always, are existential.

4.Claudio Verzilli:

you might find this page useful

http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-archive/199906/msg00025.html

5.Andre Sinclair:

This is a thorny question.  We use both quite heavily.
 Which is better depends on your priorities - we use
Splus for all statistical analysis and matlab for a
lot of our daily data processing and other automated
tasks.

Performance
---------------
I would say that if both are programmed optimally
there may not be a lot to choose in outright
performance (ok,  you could do experiments, but it
depends a lot on the problem). Both also allow linking
to C for really intensive computations. However,
matlab tends to be more manageable for large 
datasets (in my experience).  Also, for somebody who
is new to both languages I would say it will be
quicker to write reasonably fast robust code in Matlab
than in Splus.

Useability
-----------
For interactive statistical analysis of moderately
sized problems Splus win hands down, not least becuase
of the huge amount of statistical code that already
exists in it.  Also because it is more object
orientated.On the other hand, if you want to write a
robust automated process which runs every day then
choose matlab - its error trapping makes life a lot
easier among other things.

Obviously the above are my own opinions (and not my
employer's).  Undoubtedly not everyone would agree
with the above comments. I have been using Splus for 6
years and Matlab for 3.  I still find I have to think
more to solve a problem efficiently in Splus ... but
the solution is often more elegant and getting there
is more fun.  But if you don't need a lot of
statistics, or performance and robustness are
important to you then go with Matlab.

messages.subject: plot mean effects in lme
messages.body_plain:
dear s-plus users,

quite a while ago i asked for help in plotting mean effects of a
lme-model. now i finally got around to trying out josé pinheiro's
suggestion which works just perfectly. thanks a lot, josé.

bernd

>   There is no function in the NLME library that does the plot you are
>   looking for, but it's possible to write some simple S code to do it.
I
>   will use the BodyWeight data that comes with NLME (for which a model

>   essentially identical to yours is used) to illustrate it.
>
>   First the fitted object.
>
> > fm1BW.lme
> Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
>   Data: BodyWeight
>   Log-restricted-likelihood: -575.8599
>   Fixed: weight ~ Time * Diet
>  (Intercept)      Time    Diet2    Diet3 TimeDiet2 TimeDiet3
>     251.6517 0.3596391 200.6655 252.0717 0.6058392 0.2983375
>
> Random effects:
>  Formula:  ~ Time | Rat
>  Structure: General positive-definite
>                 StdDev   Corr
> (Intercept) 36.9390723 (Inter
>        Time  0.2484113 -0.149
>    Residual  4.4436052
>
> Number of Observations: 176
> Number of Groups: 16
>
> Then, you create a data.frame with the adequate values for calculating

> the fixed effects predictions. In the case of the BodyWeight data,
> because the fit is linear, we only need two time points for Diet (the
> range of the data is 1 to 64 days -- you can make it go beyond that,
> of course).
>
> > newBW <- data.frame(Time=rep(c(1,64),3),
Diet=factor(rep(1:3,c(2,2,2))))
>
> Then add the predicted values to the data (just for the fixed
effects).
>
> > newBW$pred <- predict(fm1BW.lme, newdata = newBW, level =0)
>
> Finally, use xyplot to display the curves.
>
> > xyplot(pred~Time, newBW, panel = panel.superpose, type = "l", groups
= Diet)
>
> You can make the plot prettier by assigning values to xlab and ylab,
> and specifying a legend via the "key" argument.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Transition to Splus 6.0 for Solaris
messages.body_plain:
Ted,

Online copies of the docs are distributed with the product.  If 'Splus'
is the command on your system, then run

        Splus SHOME

to see the location of the distribution directory, and then cd to that
directory.  There you can read RELNOTES.TXT and INSTALL.TXT.  Look in
the 'doc' subdirectory and all the manuals are there in pdf format.
You can read them with Adobe's Acrobat Reader (acroread).  Pay
particular attention to 'getstart.pdf'.

The basic concept you are missing is that with Splus 6, it is necessary
to initialize the data directory you are running in, e.g.:

        mkdir ted
        cd ted
        Splus CHAPTER

Thereafter, starting in the 'ted' directory will start you up there.

Whatever you do, don't try to start up in one of your old 3.4
directories.  Otherwise, you can render your data unreadable by 3.4.
(That's why you got sent to MySwork, to protect you from making that
mistake.)  Look up 'convertOldLibrary()' to see how to migrate your
existing data directories.

Good luck!

Chuck Taylor

Senior Quality Assurance Engineer       1700 Westlake Ave. N., Suite 500

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

S-Plus 6.0 (Unix) holds the documentation as pdf files under $SHOME/doc.
I can relate to your transition problem, as can all of those who've had to
make it. The documentation directory contains the following:

FIXEDBUG.TXT   instman.pdf    manl           relnotes.html  unixug.pdf
getstart.pdf   lynx_doc       model.errata   statman1.pdf
help           lynx_help      pguide.pdf     statman2.pdf

The pdf files are the various manuals. Assuming you can gain access to them,
I'd start with the Getting Started manual getstart.pdf, and then go to the
Unix User's Guide unixug.pdf, which has more information about migrating
.Data directories to be compatible with both S-Plus 6 and S-Plus 3.4 (basically,
you create two directories, one for S+6 and one for S+3.4....)

In S+6, you can create an S-Plus directory using Splus CHAPTER, which will
create a .Data directory with all the additional _* subdirectories beneath
it. Basically, it's just like 3.4 except there's extra 'stuff' :) Getting
3.4 .Data directories to be accessible in 6.0 is a bit more work, and there's
an appendix in the Unix User's Guide that discusses this in some detail.

You can get a documentation set for 6.0 from Insightful. They quoted me a
$90 price +SH, but I don't know if that's an academic price or a fixed one.
I ended up printing all the documents (approx. 2300 pages) due to time
constraints, but the point is that they are accessible to you one way or
another.

Hope this is helpful,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
In the Splus 5.0 "Getting Started" book there is a short section on
migrating from 3.4. I don't see it in the v6 getting started book.

There is a function named convertOldLibrary(). Send me a fax number
and I'll fax you a few pages.

-Don

-------------------------------------------------

First of all, a new term: "chapter".

An Splus chapter is any directory that has a subdirectory named
.Data, where the .Data directory contains __Hhelp, and the others. To
make a directory into a chapter, type the command
   Splus CHAPTER
at the unix prompt. To put it another way, a chapter is any directory
in which you have executed the "Splus CHAPTER" command.

Thereafter, when you start Splus in that directory, the local .Data
will be the default data directory. If you start Splus in a directory
that is not a chapter, it uses ~/MySwork (not MySworks). I believe it
will create ~/MySwork, and evidently already has for you, if it
doesn't exist.

You can ignore __Help, __Meta, and the others unless and until you
start doing serious programming where you use the new object-oriented
methods and/or want to write help pages for your own functions.

What I have done when I want to convert an Splus 3.4 .Data to and
Splus >=5 chapter is something relatively crude, but it has been
satisfactory to me.

At the unix prompt:
% mv .Data .Data.34
% Splus CHAPTER
% Splus
>  ## source all of the files I used to create the contents of the old .Data

This assumes, obviously, that you can reconstruct everything fairly easily.

I think I remember that Splus 6 can attach() Splus 3.4 .Data
directories and read the objects that are there. Better verify it,
though. If it does, don't try writing to those directories, though.

In any chapter you can put either or both of two special files, named
   .S.init
   .S.chapters
In .S.init put any Splus code you want to be executed every time
Splus starts up in that chapter. In .S.chapters put the name of any
chapters you want attached every time Splus starts up (don't include
the ".Data" part of the chapter name).

I recommend trying really hard to get the system admin staff to find
and loan to you some of the books that come with Splus v6. The User's
Guide and maybe the Release Notes would be the place to start.

Hope this helps.

-Don

--------------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Department
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Livermore, CA, USA
--------------------------------------

messages.subject: calculation of percentiles.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Reader of S-news,

 

I am dealing with the calculation of 50 and 90 percentiles of chemical substances in water so we can examine if certain substances exceeds some limits. The calculation could be done by a non- or by a parametrical way.The first method we usually use, because in most of the cases it is not clear what kind of distribution has to be chosen.

For the p-th percentile (say y) we estimate the i-th order:

        

i = qn+1-q 

with q = p/100 and n equals the number of nonmissing values for the variable.

Let x(1), x(2),...,x(n) represent the ordered values of the variable, then

we use for the p-th percentile (y) the weigthed average at x(i)

y = (1-f)x(k) + f*x(k+1), 

with k as the integer part of i, and f the fractional part of i.

So far so good.

But at this case we assume that every measurement is independent and has an exact representation by its value. But these values are estimated in a laboratory or we have to deal with mean values, so we know that each value has a standard error which is not always the same for each x(k). 

The question (maybe a silly statistical one):is it possible by estimating a percentile to account for the uncertainty.

with best wishes

Richard Duin

National Institute for Coastal and Marine Management

The Hague, The Netherlands

I am pleased (and relieved) to announce the publication of
Regression Modeling Strategies, With Applications to Linear
Models, Logistic Regression, and Survival Analysis
(Springer, June 2001).

This book covers a wide variety of modeling tools including
regression splines, multiple imputation, data reduction,
shrinkage, overfitting, bootstrap model validation, and

statistical properties to do what could be called 
"safe data mining."  Comprehensive case studies based on
S-Plus are presented and software for S-Plus is freely
available on many platforms.  Very soon the software
will be available for the open source R system.

Andrew,

>  -----Original Message-----

> Sent: Sunday, 22 July 2001 3:00 AM

> par(mfrow=c(2,3)) that works for plot does not seem to apply to mutiple 
> xyplots... am I missing something?

Yes you are missing something.  Trellis plotting functions (believe it or
not) do not do any plotting.  They produce trellis objects and it is the
printing of these objects that produces the plotted output.  That's why you
have to use explit calls to print() if you are trying to produce trellis
plots in loops or functions.

You should look at the help information for the function print.trellis.  The
argument postion= is used very like (but subtly different from) par(fig =
...) and the pair of arguments split= and more= are roughly equivalent to
either par(mfrow = ...) or par(mfg = ...).  I suspect you want the latter.

There is an example of this in a certain book with a bright yellow cover, I
seem to recall.

Bill Venables.

messages.body_plain:
One way to do it is to transform the matrix to a character matrix, replace
the upper (or lower) triangle with spaces or tabs and write out using
write.table. So that would look like:

x <- matrix(rnorm(100),ncol=10)
x <- matrix(as.character(x),ncol=10)
x[lower.tri(x)] <- "          "
write.table(x,file="tmp.txt", sep="")

You may need to get rid of some digits when you really want to make it look
nice.

Hope this helps,
Longhow

messages.subject: SUMMARY: S-PLUS top tips
messages.body_plain:
A while back I requested suggestions for the "Tip of the Day" in S-PLUS 6.
Thanks to everyone who responded.  A summary of the tips I received is
provided below, most of which made it into S-PLUS 6 in one form or another.
Surprisingly I only got one "frivolous" tip and unfortunately that didn't
make it into the final list (thanks anyway, Andrew!).

# David Smith

Kevin Wright [Kevin.Wright at pioneer.com]:

Q: How do I make a splom with loess lines?
A:
  panel=function(x,y,...){
    panel.xyplot(x,y,...)
    panel.loess(x,y)
  }
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q: How do I remove shading in the "strip" of a trellis plot?

strip = function(...) strip.default(..., style = 1)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q: How do I trap errors?

A: Use "try".
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q: How do I drop unused factor levels from a data.frame X?

A: For each column, do this:  X$a<-X$a[,drop=T]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bert Gunter [bert_gunter at merck.com]:

Say something about silent automatic conversion of character columns into
factors in data frames -- a frequent gotcha!

Anona Thorne (CTN) [anona at hivnet.ubc.ca]:

Since I'm using Splus 3.4 on Unix, this may or may not be useful or
relevant, but thought I'd send it along just in case.  I found it
rather subtle when I was first trying to figure it out.

If you want to have "horizontal" axis labels, i.e. labels for the
y-axis that you don't have to turn your head to read, use par(las=1)
before you create the plot.  (The default is las=0.)  This will only
work, however, if you're using the axis command without using the "at"
option.  If you don't use the "at" option, the values of crt, srt, and
adj are all ignored.

If you do use "at" to determine where your labels should appear, the
values of "las" and "side" are ignored, so you should use crt=0 in your axis
command to control the label rotation.

Naomi B. Robbins [n.robbins at att.net]:

I think that the task that gave me the most trouble was changing colors
of
graphical objects in Windows.  I see a number of questions on that in
S-News.  It's easy to change the colors under tools / color schemes.
The problem is how to let S-Plus know which color scheme you are using.
I now use the graphsheet command for that purpose, but it wasn't
immediately obvious that I should.

To turn that into a tip:

You can change the colors of graphical objects by choosing color schemes
on the tools menu.  Then use the graphsheet command to tell S-Plus which
color scheme to use.

Bill Venables [Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU]:

>>From what I see the major under-used elementary feature of S is the matrix
as index facility.  I don't know how to capture this in a tip, but here is a
weak suggestion.

----
Did you know that the elements of a k-dimensional array can be accessed in
arbitrary order by giving the array a single index that is an n x k matrix
with rows containing the actual numerical indices of the elements to be
accessed?  For example

A <- matrix(1:9, nrow=3, ncol=3)
M <- cbind(1:3, 1:3)
A[M] <- 0

replaces the diagonal entries of a 3x3 array with zeros.  In this special
case

diag(A) <- 0

does the same thing.
----

The other tips I can think of are all to do with arrays and their
manipulation.  People do not know about lower.tri, aperm, outer, &c and they
also don't know that matrix operators are often the quickest way to get
something done.  For example

The fastest way to find the row means of a matrix is
rmeans <- X %*% rep(1, ncol(X))/ncol(X)

Karen Jonson [Karen_Johnson at bd.com]:

I stumbled around S+ several months befor I came across V&R's book and the
list server.  Information on either would have saved me moutains of time.

Andrew Jack [andrew_jack at merck.com]:

"Before you spend hours trying to solve a problem, try searching the S-news
archives, or send an e-mail to the S-news list. You'll be amazed at the
response!"

"S-plus has functions called c, q, s, t, C, D, and I. So it's better not to
use these names for your own objects."

"Insightful is not such a bad name; it just takes a bit of getting used to."

"! at the start of a line sends a command to the external operating system;
otherwise, ! means logical NOT. If you want a NOT at the start of a line,
put the whole expression in parentheses"

"Don't use data frames if you have a lot of data manipulation to do; matrix
objects are much faster"

"If you're doing a lot of programming with functions, make sure you learn
how to use the browser() tool"

--

Fax: +1 (206) 283 0347

messages.subject: Re: strange round / signif behaviour
messages.body_plain:
> From: Pierre Delfosse <pierre.delfosse at centexbel.be>
> To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> Subject: [S] strange round / signif behaviour
> Date: Wed, 25 Jul 2001 14:30:53 +0200
> 
> Dear S+ users,
> 
> S+ 2000 under W98 does not always "round" nor "signif" correctly. For
> example,
> 
>       > round(0.81,2)
>       [1] 0.8100000000000001
>       > signif(0.81,2)
>       [1] 0.8100000000000001
> 
> (there are other examples).
> 
> Is this a known bug, possibly computer dependant? How can I avoid this
> behaviour?

Not a bug; it is computer dependent only in the sense that some conceivable
computer (not any in common use since binary-coded-decimal went out of style in 
the 1960's) would not have this problem.  

The number you are calculating is 0.8, but because this is not an integer
times a power of 2, it does not have an exact representation in binary
floating point.  0.8100000000000001 is as close as you can get (printed
to that degree of precision).  If you are trying to get a clean printed
representation, you should not be printing more digits than the accuracy
of the internal representation of the number.  For ordinary printing the
"digits" option give a more reasonable rounding (as long as you set it to
something reasonable (default value is 7), but with some output functions
(notably "cat")  you need to use format() to explicitly control the
number of digits printed.

Many other questions raised on this list concerning exact comparisons stem
from exactly the same type of issue.  Unless you are working with integers,
you should expect some small amount of noise in your results.

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 25 Jul 2001, Pierre Delfosse wrote:

> Dear S+ users,
>
> S+ 2000 under W98 does not always "round" nor "signif" correctly. For
> example,
>
>       > round(0.81,2)
>       [1] 0.8100000000000001
>       > signif(0.81,2)
>       [1] 0.8100000000000001
>
> (there are other examples).
>
> Is this a known bug, possibly computer dependant? How can I avoid this
> behaviour?

Well, 0.81 is not exactly representable in binary arithmetic, so a binary
computer cannot round to a number of decimal places exactly.

What you are seeing seems to be a bug in the Windows C run-time library,
*unless* you changed the `digits' option to display more than 7
significant figures.

On S+6.0, Linux, I get

> round(0.81,2)
[1] 0.81
> options(digits=16)
> round(0.81,2)
[1] 0.8100000000000001

which suggests you did not tell us the whole story.

messages.subject: Re: SUMMARY: S-PLUS top tips
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 26 Jul 2001, Henrik Aalborg Nielsen wrote:

> I'd say that the problem with functions c, q, s, t, C, D, and I is not
> that big at all:  If you make a non-function object with one of these
> names the only thing that does not work is that the function is not
> printed when it's name is typed at the prompth.  If you make a function
> which is allready there you get a warning... Or am I missing something
> here?

Yes. You only get a warning at the top level, not if you do this inside a
function.

test <- function()
{
  c <- rnorm(1)
  print(c(c, 3))
  c <- function(x) sum(x)/length(x)
  print(c(rnorm(100)))
}

> test()
[1] 1.199672 3.000000
[1] 0.05294651
[1] 0.05294651

... no warning.

Also, you can mask a function in a library section, and you will get no
warning unless the library section is currently attached.

However, I agree that this can be overplayed.  Back in the days of 3.x
it was serious.  Then S-PLUS started to check the mode and so only
functions could override functions, and in 5.x/6.x you get a warning
(which you can turn off).  But for the sake of code clarity, don't
redefine standard objects (and also to avoid a red face when you post a
mysterious error to S-news!).

messages.subject: Re: query: code for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 26 Jul 2001 Philippe.Guiblin at ons.gov.uk wrote:

> Does anyone know if there is any possibility to get Splus code able to
> perform a logistic regression model with/without random effects.

Without, glm(, family=binomial()) for the two-class class, plus lots of
interpretations (e.g. multiple logistic regression in multinom in library
nnet).

With random effects, it depends what you mean.  In full generality it is
research problem, as the integration is difficult and MCMC methods are
often used.  (Jonathan Myles had a GLMMGibbs package, but I think that is
currently only available for R.)  If the random effect is only a
per-individual intercept, then numerical quadrature can be used. (Jim
Lindsey for example has a glmm() function in that extremely restricted
sense.)  In between are PQL and other approximations: see Gordon Smyth's
code at

http://www.maths.uq.edu.au/~gks/s/index.html

(function reglm) for one example.  Searching the S-news archive should
reveal more: this has come up before.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you Tim,
Aldi

I'll enter that as an enhancement request.

Here's some example code you might adapt for your own makefiles.

DFILES=  \
allequal.d asdfasn.d asdfbnd.d asdfinf.d asdfpow.d \
(list rest of .d files)

HFILES=$(patsubst %.d, %.sgml, $(DFILES))

.d.sgml:
        doc_to_S $< > $*.sgml

This takes the .d files listed, creates a make variable containing
a list of the same files but with .sgml extension (this is needed
by other parts of the makefile), and
runs doc_to_S to create the corresponding .sgml files which are needed
for the help system.

If patsubst doesn't work for you you might have to create the
list of .sgml files by hand.

messages.subject: Labels wrong with lrm
messages.body_plain:
I get funny behaviour from lrm when using transformations that require a 
parameter, and the parameter is a variable. It only happens when there are 
other variables in the model. The transformation must be the last term in 
the formula, or some labels will be wrong. For example, if the correct 
labels are "age" "age^2" and "smok", the labels will be "age", "age^2" and 
"kx" where "kx" is actually the parameter for the transformation.

I have tried including the variable that contains the parameter for the 
transformation with datadist, but it doesn't help. Also tried reinstalling 
newest Hmisc, Design and starting new project directory. Platform: S+2000 
Win98. It happens to both rcs and pol. With glm, everything is OK. The 
value of coefficients are the same.

It isn't a major issue, but it might puzzle some and I thought I'd let you 
know. Solutions are: specify the parameters transformations directly, not 
in variables, or keep your transformations last in the formula. Any better 
solutions ? It'd be nice to be able to keep knot locations in a variable, 
so you can change it only one place in your code.

This code reproduces the problem:
library(Hmisc,T)
library(Design,T)
age <- rnorm(500,41.5,12) #age
smok <- sample(0:2,500,rep=T) #smoking habit
asthma <- sample(0:1,500,rep=T)  #asthma
mydat <- data.frame(age,smok,asthma)
dd <- datadist(mydat)
options(datadist="dd")
kx <- 2

#this model gives the wrong labels
lrm(asthma~pol(age,kx)+smok,data=mydat) 
#this model gives the right label
lrm(asthma~smok+pol(age,kx),data=mydat)

#If you don't use a variable, but a value, then everything is ok
lrm(asthma~smok+pol(age,2),data=mydat)
lrm(asthma~pol(age,2)+smok,data=mydat)
#If you only have one term, then everything is OK
lrm(asthma~pol(age,2),data=mydat)
#It doesn't happen with GLM:
glm(asthma~pol(age,2)+smok,data=mydat,family=binomial)
#but it does with rcs:
kx <- c(15,40,70)
lrm(asthma~rcs(age,kx)+smok,data=mydat) 
lrm(asthma~smok+rcs(age,kx),data=mydat) 

Jan Brogger,
University of Bergen, Norway

messages.subject: S-PLUS top tips
messages.body_plain:
David M Smith wrote:
>"S-plus has functions called c, q, s, t, C, D, and I. So it's better not to
>use these names for your own objects."

Mike Prager replied:
> For those of us with less-than-perfect memories, the easy-to-remember
> conclusion is, "So it's better never use single-letter names for your
> own objects."

I have have been using Mike's strategy for several years, especially
since there are (at least) two other letters which aren't happily used
for an object: T and F.  (Redefining them is a privilege reserved for
politicians.)  My solution is to simply take any single letter which I
was tempted to use and double it: TT, etc.  As far as I know, there
aren't any S-plus functions which are double letters.  If you find an
exception I would appreciate hearing of it.

Rick.

messages.subject: Re: R vs S/S+
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 27 Jul 2001, Ray Haraf wrote:

> Dear users,
>
> I want to learn one programming language. I have no background in
programming other than using statistical software such as SCA, TSP, SYSTAT.
I used for short period two or three modules of SAS. I'm trained in
mathematics. Given such a background should I go with S programming or
S-plus programming or R programming? What is the difference between
R and S programming? I assume S-plus is an improvement of S! Am I wrong?
What is or would be the "ideal" reference for a beginner.

A good way to look at this is that there is one langauge, `S' with three
dialects, S3, S4 and R.  S3 is available currently only on Windows, as
implemented in S-PLUS 2000.  S4 is available on Unix/Linux as S-PLUS 6.0,
and on Windows as S-PLUS 6.0 Real Soon Now (next month, I believe)

There is fairly little difference between any two of these.
So, learn the dialect for which you have an implementation (I use all
three, but S3 is clearly on its way out).   It depends a bit on your
platform: R is most widely available but with unpaid support.

As for a book, I am biased, but there is a book called `S Programming'
by Venables & R-something-or-the-other which covers all three dalects.
Whether that is the right starting point depends on whether you really
want to program or use existing applications.

The R FAQ (http://www.ci.tuwien.ac.at/~hornik/R/) may be helpful.

--

messages.subject: Re: Labels wrong with lrm
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jan,

Thank you very much for your excellent description of the
problem and the self-contained test code.  This is a
problem that I've been meaning to either document better
or solve for some time.  The root of the problem is with
the builtin S-Plus terms.inner function:

> attr(terms.inner(asthma ~ pol(age,kx) + smok),'variables')
expression(age, kx, smok)

You can see that terms.inner inappropriately includes kx
as an independent variable as it does not know that
the first argument to pol is the special variable.
When a constant replaces kx, all is well.

As I am relying on the C code called by terms.inner to 
do the job, I don't have a ready solution.  I would
be happy if someone comes up with a solution.  The
all.vars function in the R language has the same
limitation:

all.vars(asthma ~ pol(age,kx) + smok)
[1] "asthma" "age"   "kx"   "smok"

Frank Harrell

Jan Brogger wrote:
> 
> I get funny behaviour from lrm when using transformations that require a
> parameter, and the parameter is a variable. It only happens when there are
> other variables in the model. The transformation must be the last term in
> the formula, or some labels will be wrong. For example, if the correct
> labels are "age" "age^2" and "smok", the labels will be "age", "age^2" and
> "kx" where "kx" is actually the parameter for the transformation, and it
> should be "smok".
> 
> I have tried including the variable that contains the parameter for the
> transformation with datadist, but it doesn't help. Also tried reinstalling
> newest Hmisc, Design and starting new project directory. Platform: S+2000
> Win98. It happens to both rcs and pol. With glm, everything is OK. The
> value of coefficients are the same.
> 
> It isn't a major issue, but it might puzzle some and I thought I'd let you
> know. Solutions are: specify the parameters transformations directly, not
> in variables, or keep your transformations last in the formula. Any better
> solutions ? It'd be nice to be able to keep knot locations in a variable,
> so you can change it only one place in your code.
> 
> This code reproduces the problem:
> library(Hmisc,T)
> library(Design,T)
> age <- rnorm(500,41.5,12) #age
> smok <- sample(0:2,500,rep=T) #smoking habit
> asthma <- sample(0:1,500,rep=T)  #asthma
> mydat <- data.frame(age,smok,asthma)
> dd <- datadist(mydat)
> options(datadist="dd")
> kx <- 2
> 
> #this model gives the wrong labels
> lrm(asthma~pol(age,kx)+smok,data=mydat)
> #this model gives the right label
> lrm(asthma~smok+pol(age,kx),data=mydat)
> 
> #If you don't use a variable, but a value, then everything is ok
> lrm(asthma~smok+pol(age,2),data=mydat)
> lrm(asthma~pol(age,2)+smok,data=mydat)
> #If you only have one term, then everything is OK
> lrm(asthma~pol(age,2),data=mydat)
> #It doesn't happen with GLM:
> glm(asthma~pol(age,2)+smok,data=mydat,family=binomial)
> #but it does with rcs:
> kx <- c(15,40,70)
> lrm(asthma~rcs(age,kx)+smok,data=mydat)
> lrm(asthma~smok+rcs(age,kx),data=mydat)
> 
> Jan Brogger,
> University of Bergen, Norway
> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
> This message was distributed by s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu.  To
> unsubscribe send e-mail to s-news-request at lists.biostat.wustl.edu with
> the BODY of the message:  unsubscribe s-news

-- 
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

On Sat, 28 Jul 2001 fharrell at virginia.edu wrote:

> Dear Jan,
>
> Thank you very much for your excellent description of the
> problem and the self-contained test code.  This is a
> problem that I've been meaning to either document better
> or solve for some time.  The root of the problem is with
> the builtin S-Plus terms.inner function:
>
> > attr(terms.inner(asthma ~ pol(age,kx) + smok),'variables')
> expression(age, kx, smok)
>
> You can see that terms.inner inappropriately includes kx
> as an independent variable as it does not know that
> the first argument to pol is the special variable.
> When a constant replaces kx, all is well.
>
> As I am relying on the C code called by terms.inner to
> do the job, I don't have a ready solution.  I would
> be happy if someone comes up with a solution.  The
> all.vars function in the R language has the same
> limitation:
>
> all.vars(asthma ~ pol(age,kx) + smok)
> [1] "asthma" "age"   "kx"   "smok"

Well,

1) all.vars comes from S, and works the same under R.

2) I don't think it is a limitation.  all.vars is described as

Description:

     Return a character vector containing all the names which occur in
     an expression or call.

and kx is such a name.  Indeed, there is no way to know from just the
formula if it is length n-vector or a scalar.   I don't know what pol()
is, but guess it is from your library, in which case the interpretation
may well depend on where (if anywhere) that library is in the search path.

If you want special-purpose names in formulae (like strata) you need to
extend the formula-handling code.  Neither S4 nor R make that easy.

Brian
